definition.text: A graph showing how much of a good people will buy at each price, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis.

facts.text: It can show one consumer's demand or, added up across everyone, the whole market's demand.
It normally slopes down because of the law of demand; exceptions include Veblen goods, Giffen goods and speculative bubbles.
A price change moves buyers along the curve; a change in anything else, such as income, related goods' prices, population or expectations, shifts the whole curve.
When incomes rise, demand for normal goods shifts out while demand for inferior goods shifts in.
If hamburgers get dearer, demand for chicken (a substitute) shifts out and demand for ketchup (a complement) shifts in.
Demand curves are estimated statistically from past data, but only one point on the curve can be observed at any one time.

definition.text: Demand for an input that comes from demand for the final product it helps make.

facts.text: An intermediate good is one used to make another, final good.
The link is direct and positive: more demand for a final product raises demand for the inputs used to make it.

title: Effect of taxes and subsidies on price
article: Effect of taxes and subsidies on price

definition.text: How taxes and subsidies change the prices buyers pay and sellers receive, and so the quantity bought and sold.

facts.text: A tax moves the market to a new equilibrium where buyers pay more and sellers keep less.
Who legally pays the tax does not matter: a tax on sellers is largely passed on to buyers through higher prices.
Most of the burden falls on the less elastic side of the market, which is less able to change how much it buys or sells.
A specific tax shifts the supply curve up by the tax amount; an ad valorem tax, a percentage of price, also pivots it.
In one example a $0.50 tax raises the buyers' price from $3.00 to $3.30, sellers keep $2.80, and sales fall from 100 to 80.
A subsidy gives the same lower buyer price and higher seller price whether it is paid to producers or to consumers.
Tobacco taxes cut smoking: most studies find an elasticity of 0.4 to 0.5, so a 10% price rise reduces consumption by 4% to 5%.
